In the end, all this writing, and this writing is a writing with the aim of walking out along the shore into the sea, I think.

I am not in the mood for work, but I have to do something, so I turn on my computer and write a few notes. I do not want to be writing, I want to be on the beach again.

I feel the sea rising. It is as though the sea is inside me, as though the sea is in my blood and bones, and the blood and the bones are inside my skin. The wind is pushing in on the shore, and as I am writing I can feel the sea lifting in my chest and my belly and my knees and my shoulders and my toes and my back, and the wind pushing on my skin.

"I feel," I write, "that I am made out of something else, that I am built like a house, but without a foundation. I feel the sea rising and pushing against the land, but the land is not even there, it has been ripped away like a child's building blocks and the sea now builds around me, and I am this sea. The sky and the waves are built around me and I am this."

Then I sit at my desk and wait, and the sea is rising and the sky is falling and I sit for a long time in my little house, and the wind blows in through the window and around the corner of the desk and over the book of poems and into me. I am the sea, and I am the sky, and I am the house that is the ocean. I am a child, and the sea is my womb, and I am the mother of the sea.

When I get up I go down to the beach. I walk all the way out to the edge of the water and sit there, and watch the sun come up behind the mountains, and the light plays on the waves.
